background.definition: Toilet training is a process by which children learn to complete controlled stooling and urination on the toilet.

list.listitem: The trend toward later toilet training is associated with increased financial expense and the increased environmental burden of nonbiodegradable materials due to prolonged diaper use.
Toilet training is a complex developmental process that combines physiologic maturity with social and psychological readiness.
There is significant variation in toilet training practices across cultures.

Toilet training requires the physiologic maturity to attain bowel and bladder continence. Completion of toilet training is occurring at older ages than in the past due to later age at initiation of toilet training, frequent refusals to stool on the toilet, and the frequent occurrence of constipation.

Normative data about the sequential acquisition of toilet training skills among normal children can provide physicians with information to use when counseling parents about readiness for toilet training ().
Girls achieve almost all toilet training skills earlier than boys.
Evaluate the child for cognitive, bladder, bowel, and motor readiness. C
No diagnostic tests are indicated unless the physical examination reveals abnormal findings or the child is older than 36 months and shows no signs of voluntary bladder control. C
The median age that toilet training skills are acquired is shown in . The signs of toilet training readiness most commonly cited by pediatricians are shown in .
A child demonstrates cognitive readiness for toilet training by understanding the purpose of the potty and showing interest in using the potty.
A child demonstrates bladder readiness for toilet training by recognizing the need to void and briefly delaying the need to urinate.
A child demonstrates bowel readiness for toilet training by recognizing the need to stool and briefly delaying the urge to stool.
A child demonstrates motor readiness for toilet training by getting on and off the potty chair.
Constipation frequently precedes a first episode of stool toileting refusal.

Assess the child's history of demonstrating common toilet training readiness signs, evaluate the child's physical strength and motor control, and assess the parent's expectations about toilet training.
Evaluate the parent's perception of the child's readiness for training.
Most importantly, correct any misalignment between the parent's perception and the child's demonstrated readiness.
Studies of the timing of the development of toileting skills indicate that most children do not master the readiness skills of toilet training until after 24 months of age. B
There is no strong evidence favoring child-oriented versus structured behavioral approaches.C
There is little benefit to initiating intensive toilet training prior to 27 months of age.

There are two predominant theories of toilet training in the United States. In the child-oriented gradual training approach, toilet training is accomplished as a gradual progression of the parent recognizing and responding to the child's signs of toilet readiness. The child-oriented approach was first described by T. Berry Brazelton in 1962. This is the most common approach recommended by pediatricians (72%).

In the structured behavioral approach, toilet training is accomplished by a process of operant conditioning to teach a specific sequence of independent toileting behaviors. This approach may also be referred to as the "intensive" approach.

A systematic review concluded that the structured behavioral approach is more frequently used, but that the age of completion of toilet training is similar between structured and child-oriented approaches. Success rates were sparsely reported in the literature but appeared to be better with the child-oriented approach.

Parents frequently seek the advice of physicians regarding the process of toilet training. Unfortunately for health care providers and parents, there is very little evidence in the medical literature comparing the two methods. A review of the literature reveals no consensus on optimal age at which to initiate toilet training or the mean expected duration of toilet training. Physicians are left with little evidence upon which to base their recommendation to parents on the topic of toilet training.
Children who have a history of constipation or who hide while stooling may be more difficult to toilet train.
The majority of children will complete toilet training by 36 months of age if toilet training is initiated by 27 months of age. C
Difficulties with toilet training can be predicted for children who hide while stooling, who have a history of constipation, and who are characterized as less adaptable. B

feature.caption: Signs of Toilet Training Readiness.
feature.feature_body: Child is aware that he/she is wet/soiled. Child can communicate need to void or stool. Child physically able to sit on toilet. Child physically able to pull pants down/up. Child shows an interest in toilet. Child understands toileting-related terms. Data from Polaha J, Warzak WJ, Dittmer-McMahon K.
